opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about that illustration a lot. Bill Freeman has this slide, I believe it's from his talk on how to do research, where he plots paper quality on the x-axis and the impact on your career on the y-axis. Most people intuitively imagine a straight line, where every paper adds a little bit. But his curve is very nonlinear. For a long stretch, mediocre or just "okay" papers contribute almost nothing. They're basically flat near zero. Then at the very high end, the curve shoots up. A small number of really excellent pieces of work account for almost all of the impact.

To me, the lesson is that research isn't an accumulation game. You don't build a career by stacking up a lot of incremental papers. People remember you for one or two things that changed how the field thinks or works. Many people end up being known for a single paper, and that's fine. That's how it works.

This affects how I choose problems. As a student, especially in a field moving as fast as AI, there's huge pressure to publish a lot, hit every deadline, and keep the paper count going up. It feels productive. But if you take Bill's curve seriously, much of that effort lands in the flat region. It doesn't really move anything. It's better to spend a long time on something you truly believe in, something that could be a real step forward, even if it's riskier and might take a year or more.

There's another subtle point. The curve isn't only about your career. It's about the field too. A sea of mediocre papers creates noise, and everyone has to wade through it. One clear, solid, simple idea that works is worth much more than ten papers that each add half a point on a benchmark.

Of course, this is easy to say and hard to do. You can't know ahead of time which project will land in the steep part of the curve. So it's partly about taste, and partly about courage: being willing to not publish for a while, to say no to safe projects, and to bet on directions that feel important. When I mentor students now, I try to pass that on. Don't optimize for the count. Aim for the work you'd be proud to be remembered for.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes the curve as nonlinear, with a long flat region followed by a sharp rise.

r002.rationale: The response says mediocre or okay papers contribute almost nothing, but does not clearly state that very poor research generally does little harm to a career.

r003.rationale: The response says mediocre or okay papers contribute almost nothing to career impact, conveying little benefit from fairly good research.

fable-5.1.text:
Bill Freeman had this illustration that I think about all the time. It's a simple plot. On one axis you have the quality of a research project, and on the other axis you have the impact it has on your career. And the key thing is that the curve is not linear. It's not that if you do a project that's twice as good, you get twice the reward. It's more like a step function, or even exponential. Most projects, even solid, competent ones, land in this flat region where they basically contribute very little. And then there's a small number of projects that cross some threshold, and those are the ones that define your career.

When I first saw it as a student, honestly it was a little depressing, because it means a lot of the incremental work we do doesn't really matter that much in the long run. But I've come to see it as liberating. It tells you where to put your energy. The rational strategy is not to produce many "okay" papers. It's to be willing to spend a long time, maybe take a lot of risk, to try to get one or two things into that upper region. You can fail a lot, and that's fine, because the failures sit in the same flat zone as the mediocre successes anyway.

For me, ResNeXt and ConvNeXt and the work on diffusion transformers were examples of that. None of them came from chasing a trend of the moment. They came from asking a question I actually found uncomfortable, like, "Do we really understand why this works, or are we just accepting it?" and then being stubborn about it. The illustration gave me permission to be stubborn. It also shaped how I advise students now. I tell them, don't optimize for the next deadline. Optimize for the one project that, ten years later, people still cite not because they have to, but because it changed how they think.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the quality-to-career-impact curve is “not linear.”

r002.rationale: It says failures sit in the same low-impact flat zone as mediocre successes and that “you can fail a lot” and be fine, communicating little career harm from very poor research.

r003.rationale: It says even “solid, competent” projects land in a flat region and contribute very little, indicating little career benefit from fairly good research.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that research quality and career impact are related, but they’re not the same thing. The quality of a piece of work is about whether it gives us a meaningful insight or solves an important problem. Career impact also depends on whether people recognize that contribution, which can involve timing, visibility, and how clearly you communicate it.

So I wouldn’t treat the attention a paper receives as a perfect measure of its quality. Good work can take time to be appreciated. For me, the useful takeaway is to focus on doing work that has lasting value, while also making it understandable to others. You can influence how your work is received, but you can’t completely control it.

r001.rationale: It says research quality and career impact are related but not the same, without stating that their relationship is nonlinear.

r002.rationale: It does not say that very poor research generally does little harm to a researcher’s career.

r003.rationale: It does not say that fairly good research brings little career benefit.

sol-6.1.text: The way I understand Bill Freeman’s illustration is that research quality and career impact are related, but they’re not the same thing. You can do very good work that doesn’t immediately attract much attention, and a project can have a big career impact partly because of timing or visibility. So you shouldn’t use the response to a single paper as a verdict on your ability as a researcher. What you can keep working on is the quality of your questions and how convincingly you answer them. You hope that translates into impact over time, but you can’t control that relationship completely.
